svg.title: Interpreter
svg.desc: Interpreter. Represent a small language's grammar as classes and evaluate a sentence by walking its syntax tree. Step 1, Rules frozen in code: Targeting lives in nested ifs in FlagService: each change is a code edit and a deploy, for everyone. Step 2, Grammar as classes: Each grammar rule becomes a class with interpret(ctx), and the rule text is parsed once into a tree. Step 3, Evaluate against a context: interpret(ctx) runs down the tree and each node returns true or false: #1 is true, #2 and #3 false. Step 4, Small languages only: Rules are now data, changed without a deploy. Keep the grammar small, and never eval() user rules.

g.text: Targeting lives in nested ifs in FlagService: each change is a code edit and a deploy, for everyone.
Each grammar rule becomes a class with interpret(ctx), and the rule text is parsed once into a tree.
interpret(ctx) runs down the tree and each node returns true or false: #1 is true, #2 and #3 false.
Rules are now data, changed without a deploy. Keep the grammar small, and never eval() user rules.
Every flag's targeting is code that ships with the service
Open new-checkout to MY too, and to teams over 5 seats
Acme wants new-checkout only for plan = 'enterprise'
✗ One rule in code, the same for every customer
Every rule change is a release of the service
Targeting rule · flag new-checkout · saved as text
Parsed once, when the rule is saved: a tree of objects whose classes all implement Expr
interpret(ctx) goes down the tree and true or false comes back up; And stops at the first false
Rules as data: a change is a text edit, no deploy; per customer too
Small grammars: each new construct is a class and a parser change
Bigger languages: a real parser, then compile to closures or bytecode
User-written rules: never eval() them; cap nesting, size and run time
In use: feature-flag targeting · OPA's Rego · CEL in Kubernetes and Envoy · regex engines · SQL WHERE clauses
